questions.stem: The 19th-century ideology of 'separate spheres' held that:
options: upper-class women should work in factories to set an example to the poor
men belonged in public life and paid work, women in the home and family
women and men should hold equal places in politics, work and the home
married women should run family businesses while men served in the army
questions.explanation: Separate spheres assigned the public world of politics, business and paid work to men and the private, domestic world to women, who were seen as the moral guardians of the home. The idea was strongest among the middle classes; many working-class women had to earn wages regardless.

questions.stem: Before the Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 in Britain, a married woman's legal position was shaped mainly by the doctrine of coverture, under which:
options: she kept full ownership of her property but could not vote in elections
her father kept legal control of her property until she turned thirty
she could own property only if she had no children under the age of ten
her property and earnings passed to her husband's control on marriage
questions.explanation: Under coverture a wife's legal identity was absorbed into her husband's, so her property and wages came under his control. The 1870 Act let wives keep their own earnings and the 1882 Act let them own and control property in their own right.

questions.stem: The Declaration of Sentiments, adopted at the Seneca Falls Convention in New York in 1848, is significant because it:
options: rejected the demand for the vote and focused only on women's access to university education
modelled itself on the Declaration of Independence to list women's grievances and demand equal rights
won American women the vote in federal elections within a few years of the convention meeting
was the first international treaty to recognise married women's right to own property and to seek divorce
questions.explanation: Drafted mainly by Elizabeth Cady Stanton, it began by declaring that all men and women are created equal and listed grievances, including the denial of the vote. American women did not win the federal vote until the 19th Amendment of 1920.

questions.stem: Which was the first self-governing country to give women the vote in national elections, in 1893?
options: United Kingdom
New Zealand
Australia
Finland
questions.explanation: New Zealand women won the vote in 1893, although they could not stand for parliament until 1919. South Australian women won both rights in 1894, and the Commonwealth followed in 1902. Finland gave women the vote in 1906.

questions.stem: In Britain, the National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies, led by Millicent Fawcett, differed from the suffragettes mainly because it:
options: used peaceful, lawful methods such as petitions, meetings and lobbying
demanded the vote for all adult women at once rather than for some women
refused to cooperate with any male politicians or political parties at all
campaigned for the vote in local councils only, not in parliamentary elections
questions.explanation: The suffragists of the NUWSS, founded in 1897, relied on constitutional methods and became the largest suffrage organisation. The suffragettes of the WSPU turned to militant action such as window-smashing and arson.

questions.stem: In 1913 the British government passed the Prisoners (Temporary Discharge for Ill-Health) Act, known as the 'Cat and Mouse Act'. It allowed the authorities to:
options: release hunger-striking suffragettes when weak and re-arrest them once they recovered
force-feed any suffragette prisoner who refused food for more than a single day
deport suffragette leaders to the colonies if they were convicted of arson twice
ban suffragette newspapers and close the offices of the Women's Social and Political Union
questions.explanation: Force-feeding hunger strikers, used from 1909, had caused public outrage. The Act let the government release prisoners before they became dangerously ill and then return them to prison, so they would not become martyrs by dying in custody.

questions.stem: Emily Wilding Davison died in June 1913 after she:
options: was caught in a fire she had lit at the house of the Chancellor of the Exchequer
ran onto the course at the Epsom Derby and was struck by the King's horse
was force-fed in Holloway prison during a long hunger strike against her sentence
was injured when police broke up a suffragette march to the Houses of Parliament
questions.explanation: Davison stepped in front of the King's horse, Anmer, at the Derby on 4 June 1913 and died of her injuries four days later. Her funeral became a large suffragette procession. Historians still debate whether she meant to die or to attach a banner to the horse.

questions.stem: Under Britain's Representation of the People Act 1918, which women gained the parliamentary vote?
options: All women over 21, on the same terms as men, without any property qualification
Only women who had served in the armed forces or in munitions work during the war
Only unmarried women over 25 who paid income tax and owned their own houses
Women over 30 who met a property qualification or were married to a man who did
questions.explanation: The 1918 Act gave the vote to most men over 21 but only to women over 30 who met property conditions, about 8.4 million women. Equal voting at 21 came with the Equal Franchise Act 1928.

questions.stem: Historians debate why British women won the vote in 1918. Which argument best challenges the view that the vote was simply a reward for women's war work?
options: The leaders of the Women's Social and Political Union supported the war effort from 1914
Parliament also gave the vote to many men who had fought but had previously lacked it
The women enfranchised were mostly over 30, while many young munitions workers stayed voteless
Large numbers of women had worked in factories, on transport and in nursing between 1914 and 1918
questions.explanation: Most munitions workers were young, single women who did not qualify under the age and property rules, which weakens the 'reward' explanation. Historians also point to pre-war campaigning, fear of renewed militancy and the need to reform the franchise for returning soldiers. The other points are true but do not undermine the reward argument.

questions.stem: How did the First World War affect women's work in Britain and Australia?
options: Women were paid at the same rates as men, and equal pay continued after the war ended
Married women were banned from paid work so that jobs could be kept for returning soldiers
Many women took jobs in industry, transport and offices, though most war jobs ended in 1918-19
Women were conscripted into the armed forces and many served in combat roles on the Western Front
questions.explanation: Women filled many jobs left by men, especially in Britain's munitions factories. They were usually paid less than men, and most were expected to give their jobs back to returning servicemen. Women served in uniform as nurses and auxiliaries, not in combat.

questions.stem: In 1942 the Australian Government set up the Women's Employment Board. What does its role suggest about the Second World War's effect on women's status?
options: The government wanted women out of the workforce, so the Board limited them to unpaid volunteer work
Trade unions had already won equal pay before the war, so the Board simply recorded existing rates
Wartime need led the state to raise some women's wages towards male rates, but only in certain jobs
The war ended unequal pay in Australia, since all women were paid the full male rate from 1942
questions.explanation: The Board set pay for women doing work previously done by men, often at a higher share of the male rate than usual. The change was temporary and limited, and general equal pay did not come until the 1969 and 1972 equal pay cases.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the experience of many women in Western countries in the late 1940s and 1950s?
options: Governments made childcare free so that mothers could keep the jobs they had held in the war
The baby boom ended as women chose careers over marriage in record numbers across the West
Many left wartime jobs and an ideal of the suburban housewife and mother was widely promoted
Most married women stayed in full-time paid work at the same pay rates as their husbands
questions.explanation: Postwar culture celebrated domesticity, and the baby boom and growth of suburbs reinforced the housewife ideal. Yet the number of married women in paid work gradually rose through the 1950s, which helped create the tensions second-wave feminists later voiced.

questions.stem: The oral contraceptive pill became available in Australia in:
questions.explanation: The pill was approved in the USA in 1960 and became available in Australia in 1961. By giving women more reliable control over pregnancy, it made it easier to plan education and careers.

questions.stem: Which postwar development most directly increased the number of married women in paid work in Western countries?
options: Laws that required all mothers of school-age children to find paid work
The closure of most girls' schools, which pushed young women into jobs
Growth in clerical, retail and service jobs, along with smaller families
The return of heavy industry jobs that men had filled during the war years
questions.explanation: The expanding service economy created many office, shop and service jobs, and smaller families meant women spent fewer years caring for infants. Labour-saving appliances also reduced housework time, though women still did most of it.

questions.stem: A historian notes that washing machines and refrigerators spread rapidly in postwar homes, yet surveys found full-time housewives' hours of housework barely fell. Which conclusion best fits this evidence?
options: Men took over most domestic tasks once machines made the work physically easier to do
Governments rationed electricity to homes, so families seldom used the new appliances
Appliances changed housework but rising standards of cleanliness and care absorbed the time saved
Appliances were too expensive for most families, so very few homes had them before the 1980s
questions.explanation: Historians of technology have argued that appliances raised expectations, such as more frequent washing and more elaborate meals, rather than freeing large amounts of time. The finding supports the view that technology alone did not change gender roles.

questions.stem: Betty Friedan's 1963 book The Feminine Mystique argued that:
options: many educated American housewives were unfulfilled by a life limited to home and family
women should withdraw from paid work to protect their families from the effects of economic recession
women had already achieved full equality and no longer needed a political movement
only working-class women suffered discrimination, while middle-class women did not
questions.explanation: Friedan described 'the problem that has no name': the dissatisfaction of many suburban housewives. The book became a bestseller and helped spark second-wave feminism in the USA.

questions.stem: In 1966 Betty Friedan helped found the National Organization for Women (NOW). Its main approach was to:
options: form women-only communes that rejected all contact with mainstream politics
campaign against married women entering higher education and the professional careers
support the conscription of women into the US armed forces during wartime
lobby and take legal action for equal rights in employment, education and the law
questions.explanation: NOW, with Friedan as its first president, pressed governments to enforce the ban on sex discrimination in the Civil Rights Act 1964 and campaigned for the Equal Rights Amendment. It represented the liberal, reformist wing of the movement.

questions.stem: The slogan 'the personal is political', used by many women's liberation groups from about 1970, meant that:
options: politicians' personal lives should be kept out of newspapers and election campaigns
only women who held political office could speak for the women's movement as a whole
issues in private life, such as housework, sexuality and violence, reflected wider power structures
women should keep their personal views private and never raise them in political meetings or rallies
questions.explanation: Women's liberation groups argued that problems women experienced as individual, such as domestic violence or the unequal division of housework, were shaped by society and could be changed by political action. Consciousness-raising groups grew from this idea.

questions.stem: Protesters at the 1968 Miss America pageant in Atlantic City threw bras, high heels and make-up into a 'Freedom Trash Can'. What is the best-supported fact about this protest?
options: The pageant was cancelled and never held again because of the demonstration
It was organised by Betty Friedan's NOW as its first national campaign
No bras were burned there; the label 'bra-burners' came from media reports
Police banned the protest, so it took place in secret with no reporters present
questions.explanation: The protesters had planned to set the bin alight but did not have a permit to do so. Press coverage nonetheless linked the protest to burning bras, and 'bra-burner' became a dismissive label for feminists.

questions.stem: The Women's Electoral Lobby (WEL), founded in Australia in 1972, is best known for:
options: running its own candidates for the Senate in every state at the 1972 election
campaigning to restore the marriage bar in the Commonwealth Public Service
organising militant protests that smashed the windows of Parliament House
surveying election candidates on women's issues and publishing their answers
questions.explanation: Before the 1972 federal election WEL questioned candidates on issues such as equal pay, childcare and abortion law and published the results. It continued as a non-party lobby group.

questions.stem: Germaine Greer's The Female Eunuch (1970) is associated with the women's liberation strand of feminism because it:
options: argued that legal reforms alone would bring full equality without changes in attitudes
called on women to leave paid work and return to the home as full-time mothers
rejected all public campaigning in favour of quiet study within universities
urged women to free themselves from the roles and self-images society imposed on them
questions.explanation: Greer argued that women had been taught to accept passive, limiting roles and encouraged them to reject them. Liberationists sought deep cultural change, while liberal feminists such as NOW focused more on legal and economic equality.

questions.stem: Which pair best shows the difference between 'equal pay for equal work' and 'equal pay for work of equal value' in Australia's equal pay decisions?
options: 1969 covered women doing the same job as men; 1972 extended equal pay to jobs mainly done by women
1969 applied only to the public service; 1972 applied only to private employers in factories
1969 gave women 75 per cent of the male wage; 1972 raised it to 90 per cent of the male wage
1969 covered only married women; 1972 extended the same rule to single women and widows
questions.explanation: The 1969 decision helped only women doing the same work as men, which few did, since the workforce was largely segregated by sex. The 1972 principle of work of equal value let female-dominated jobs be compared with male jobs, so it reached far more women.

questions.stem: Which Commonwealth law of 1984 made sex discrimination in areas such as employment and education unlawful across Australia?
options: the Sex Discrimination Act
the Family Law Act
the Equal Franchise Act
the Conciliation and Arbitration Act
questions.explanation: The Sex Discrimination Act 1984 banned discrimination on the grounds of sex, marital status and pregnancy, and sexual harassment. The Family Law Act 1975 introduced no-fault divorce.

questions.stem: Until 1966, a woman who married while working in the Commonwealth Public Service had to resign her permanent position. This rule is an example of:
options: an affirmative action policy designed to open jobs to young women
a wartime regulation that was cancelled as soon as peace returned
a trade union demand to protect married women's health at work
a marriage bar that reinforced the role of the male breadwinner
questions.explanation: The marriage bar assumed that a husband should support his wife and that married women belonged at home. Its removal in 1966 was an early sign of changing attitudes to gender roles in Australia.

questions.stem: Who became the world's first woman prime minister, in Ceylon (now Sri Lanka) in 1960?
options: Golda Meir
Chandrika Kumaratunga
Sirimavo Bandaranaike
Indira Gandhi
questions.explanation: Sirimavo Bandaranaike became prime minister of Ceylon in 1960. Indira Gandhi led India from 1966, Golda Meir led Israel from 1969, and Bandaranaike's daughter Chandrika Kumaratunga became prime minister of Sri Lanka in 1994.

questions.stem: A student claims that women prime ministers such as Bandaranaike, Indira Gandhi and Margaret Thatcher prove that women's movements had achieved equality by the 1980s. Which point most weakens this claim?
options: Several came from political families, and women stayed a small minority of MPs in most countries
Each of them won office at elections in which women had the right to vote and to stand
They led countries in different regions of the world with very different economic systems
Some of them held office for more than ten years and won several general elections in a row
questions.explanation: Bandaranaike and Gandhi rose partly through family connections, and in most parliaments women held only a small share of seats for decades. A few prominent leaders did not mean equal representation. The other points do not test the claim.

questions.stem: When India's Constitution came into force in 1950, women gained:
options: the vote only after a later amendment passed in the 1970s
the vote on the same terms as men under universal adult suffrage
the vote only if they owned land or had completed secondary school
the vote in local elections but not in elections for the national parliament
questions.explanation: The Constitution gave all adult citizens the vote from the start, so Indian women did not have to fight a separate suffrage campaign after independence. Women had been active in the nationalist movement, including Gandhi's civil disobedience campaigns.

questions.stem: The Self-Employed Women's Association (SEWA), founded by Ela Bhatt in Ahmedabad in 1972, is significant because it:
options: organised poor women in informal work, such as vendors and home-based workers, as a union
campaigned for women to be admitted to the Indian Army as combat officers and pilots
was the first group to demand the vote for Indian women after independence in 1947
ran schools that trained upper-caste women to enter the Indian civil service
questions.explanation: SEWA showed that women outside formal employment could organise for fair pay, credit and social security. It also founded a cooperative bank for its members and became a model for organising informal workers.

questions.stem: In the late 1970s and 1980s, Indian women's groups campaigned strongly against dowry-related violence. This campaign shows that the Indian movement:
options: had no connection with Western feminism or with international women's organisations
focused on family customs and violence that the law already banned but failed to stop
copied the British suffragettes' demand for the vote, which Indian women still lacked
rejected all legal change and relied only on religious leaders to end the practice
questions.explanation: Dowry had been banned by the Dowry Prohibition Act 1961, yet dowry demands and deaths continued. Protests drew attention to the gap between law and practice and led to stronger laws in the 1980s. Indian women already had the vote.

questions.stem: In 1985 India's Supreme Court ruled in the Shah Bano case that a divorced Muslim woman was entitled to maintenance from her former husband. In 1986 Parliament passed a law that limited the effect of the ruling. What issue does this episode best illustrate?
options: The power of the British Privy Council over Indian court decisions
Tension between women's rights and religious community personal laws
The refusal of Indian courts to hear cases brought by women at all
The success of women's groups in ending all religious family law
questions.explanation: The ruling angered conservative Muslim leaders, and the government responded with the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act 1986. Women's groups saw this as putting community politics ahead of women's rights. India's courts were fully independent of Britain by then.

questions.stem: The 73rd Amendment to India's Constitution (1992) advanced women's political participation by:
options: reserving one-third of seats in village councils (panchayats) for women
requiring the Prime Minister to appoint women to half of all cabinet posts
lowering the voting age for women to 18 while it stayed at 21 for men
creating a separate women's parliament with power to veto national laws
questions.explanation: The reservation brought large numbers of women into local government across rural India. Some states later raised the share to half of seats.

questions.stem: Which argument did the American conservative Phyllis Schlafly use in her STOP ERA campaign against the Equal Rights Amendment in the 1970s?
options: It had already been ratified by every state, so a further campaign for it was pointless
It would remove legal protections for housewives and could make women liable for the military draft
It would give women too few rights, so feminists should demand a stronger amendment instead
It would cost too much to print new ballot papers for women voting in federal elections
questions.explanation: Schlafly argued the amendment would undermine the traditional family and the support owed to wives and mothers. The ERA passed Congress in 1972 but fell three states short of the 38 needed for ratification by the 1982 deadline.

questions.stem: In Britain in 1908, opponents of votes for women formed the:
options: Women's Freedom League
National Union of Women's Suffrage Societies
National Union of Women Workers
Women's National Anti-Suffrage League
questions.explanation: The Anti-Suffrage League, whose leaders included the novelist Mary Humphry Ward, argued that women's influence belonged in the home and local affairs, not national politics. Its existence shows that many women as well as men opposed suffrage. The NUWSS, by contrast, was the main pro-suffrage body, founded in 1897.

questions.stem: The #MeToo movement spread worldwide in October 2017. Which statement about it is accurate?
options: It began as a campaign by a political party to win seats in the US Congress
It was limited to the USA and had little effect on public debate in other countries
It focused mainly on winning the vote for women in countries that still denied it
Activist Tarana Burke had used the phrase from 2006, before it spread on social media
questions.explanation: Burke began using 'Me Too' in 2006 to support survivors of sexual violence. After allegations against film producer Harvey Weinstein in 2017, the hashtag spread across many countries, raising demands about workplace harassment and accountability.

questions.stem: Which list best represents the main demands of women's movements in the 21st century?
options: Restoring the marriage bar, ending childcare funding and lowering women's wages to cut costs
Abolishing all anti-discrimination laws and returning control of family law to the churches and courts
Closing the gender pay gap, ending gendered violence and harassment, and equal representation
Winning the vote, the right to own property and entry to universities and the professions
questions.explanation: With legal equality largely won in Western countries, recent movements focus on persistent gaps in pay and leadership and on violence and harassment. Votes, property rights and education access were 19th- and early 20th-century demands.

questions.stem: Some historians criticise describing feminism as 'waves' (first wave suffrage, second wave 1960s-70s). Which criticism is most commonly made?
options: It gives too much attention to women outside Europe and North America and to working women
It wrongly claims that women won the vote in most Western countries before the year 1850
It treats the suffrage movement as more militant than the movements of the 1960s and 1970s
It hides activism between the waves and centres white, middle-class Western women
questions.explanation: Critics argue that the metaphor suggests the movement disappeared between the 1920s and 1960s, when women kept campaigning on pay, work and welfare, and that it centres the story on white Western women. The opposite of the second option is the usual complaint.

questions.stem: In 1989 the legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw introduced the term 'intersectionality'. It refers to:
options: how overlapping identities such as race, class and gender combine to shape discrimination
the point at which the first and second waves of feminism met in the late 1950s
the legal principle that men and women must receive identical treatment at work
an alliance between women's movements and trade unions to win equal pay rates
questions.explanation: Crenshaw argued that Black women could face discrimination that neither anti-racist nor feminist frameworks alone captured. The idea has shaped 21st-century feminism and criticism of earlier movements that spoke mainly for white women.

questions.stem: A historian argues that the suffragettes' militancy after 1912 delayed votes for women. Which evidence would best support this interpretation?
options: Membership of the peaceful NUWSS was far larger than that of the WSPU by the year 1914
The WSPU called off its militant campaign at the outbreak of war in August 1914
Suffragette newspapers sold tens of thousands of copies each week before the war
MPs who had backed suffrage bills cited arson and window-smashing as reasons to vote against them
questions.explanation: This interpretation rests on evidence that militancy alienated politicians and the public; some MPs explicitly said they would not reward violence. The size of the NUWSS shows the strength of peaceful campaigning but does not by itself show militancy caused delay.
